query: For bulk HfNbTaTiZr, what testable hypothesis could an unspecified predictive approach make to overcome the limited accuracy of available analytical predictions and their usual restriction to perfect, defect-free crystals? Address the nearly 0–200 K regime and the 300–1200 K regime, for which measurements also exist on a specimen containing 1 wt.% oxygen; explain why the approach should improve accuracy, predict its advantage over existing analytical approaches, define its temperature and sample applicability limits, identify supporting prior evidence, and specify a held-out conductivity benchmark and result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: An explainable ML model that explicitly incorporates microstructural defect levels and oxygen contamination as features will yield more accurate predictions of conductivity in bulk HfNbTaTiZr across both low (0–200 K) and high (300–1200 K) temperature regimes than conventional analytical approaches that assume perfect, defect‐free crystals.
generation.material_initial_state: Bulk HfNbTaTiZr alloy, where the initial state can vary between nearly perfect crystalline structures (defect‐free) and samples intentionally doped with 1 wt.% oxygen to introduce extrinsic defects.
generation.intervention: Develop and apply an interpretable machine learning framework that uses experimental data from simpler alloy systems (e.g., binary alloys) along with measured defect and oxygen impurity data to predict conductivity. This framework is then applied to bulk HfNbTaTiZr samples.
generation.conditions: Measurements conducted in two regimes: (a) cryogenic (0–200 K), where defect‐induced scattering dominates, and (b) high-temperature (300–1200 K), where phonon scattering is dominant. Both nearly defect-free and 1 wt.% oxygen‐contaminated specimens should be tested.
generation.structural_mediator: The presence of microstructural defects and oxygen impurity phases, which modify electron/phonon scattering rates in the alloy.
generation.mechanism: Including explicit microstructural descriptors (defect density, impurity concentration) in the ML model allows it to capture the additional scattering effects not accounted for in ideal, defect-free analytical models. This should better reflect the real transport behavior of the alloy by adjusting predictions based on actual microstructural imperfections.
generation.predicted_outcome: The ML model will predict lower conductivity for the oxygen-contaminated specimens compared to defect-free predictions, especially at low temperatures where defect scattering is critical. Overall, the predictions will align more closely with experimental measurements, achieving an improvement in predictive accuracy (on the order of ~10–15% lower error margin) relative to conventional models.
generation.baseline: Analytical prediction methods that assume perfect, defect-free crystalline models and do not account for scattering from defects or oxygen impurities.
generation.boundary: The approach is applicable for bulk HfNbTaTiZr samples tested in the 0–200 K and 300–1200 K regimes. Its accuracy is expected to degrade outside these temperature ranges or if oxygen contamination far exceeds 1 wt.% (or if other unaccounted impurities dominate the defect structure).
generation.uncertainty: Quantitative improvements in prediction accuracy (exact percentage improvement and absolute conductivity changes) are not fully established until experimental validation is performed. The degree to which defect and oxygen data enhance the model also remains to be determined.

falsification_experiment.design: Fabricate bulk HfNbTaTiZr samples under two conditions: (i) near defect-free and (ii) with controlled 1 wt.% oxygen addition. Measure thermal or electrical conductivity over the temperature ranges 0–200 K and 300–1200 K. Compare the performance of predictions made using the ML-based model (incorporating defect/oxygen features) with that of conventional defect-free analytical predictions.
measurements: Microstructural characterization (using TEM or XRD for defect density)
Oxygen content verification (using techniques such as combustion analysis or XPS)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the ML model’s predictions do not show a statistically significant reduction in prediction error (e.g., less than a ~10–15% improvement over conventional models across both temperature regimes) or fail to account for the reduced conductivity in the oxygen-doped samples, the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Each approach to alloy design (selection) that has been discussed above would give an alloy composition for which solidification path, volume fractions of phases and phase equilibria at different temperatures could be calculated, provided thermodynamic data was available. This task is not possible currently, for the reasons discussed in the introduction. Using knowledge gained from on-going research it is possible to make some informed predictions for the selected alloys. The latter and the calculated (predicted) properties can be tested experimentally. For example, the alloy A should have βNb5Si3 as its primary phase, in its microstructure tetragonal Nb5Si3 and Nbss should be stable at 1500 °C but not the C14 NbCr2 Laves and A15 intermetallic phases and the alloy should not pest. The alloy B should have βNb5Si3 as its primary phase, eutectic with Nbss and Nb5Si3 should form (see below), in its microstructure tetragonal Nb5Si3, Nbss (most likely solid solution with no Si) and A15 intermetallic should be stable at 1500 °C but not C14 NbCr2 Laves phase and the alloy should not pest.

Machine learning (ML) techniques have been actively utilized for various applications in recent years due to their superior prediction performance. However, as the applications expand vastly, they also have been required to meet the demand of high level of transparency and accountability due to their black-box framework. As a result, explainable ML methods have attracted a great deal of attention in order to further advance the reliability and applicability of ML-based approaches. Model explainability is also becoming increasingly important in the materials science domain as ML and artificial intelligence (AI)-driven algorithms are beginning to show success in simplifying various workflows. However, the idea of incorporating explainable ML methods into the current data-driven materials design and discovery workflow is still in its infancy. Unlike many other disciplines, materials science suffers from limited and sparse data. Incorporating interpretablility into the black-box ML models make it possible to explain the ML predictions with more confidence, especially when the models are trained using small and heterogeneous datasets.
